title: A slice of history from JC's Pizzaria, closing after 42 years in Keizer - NewsBreak
text: The nostalgia is undeniable when you walk into JC’s Pizzaria. Little League trophies dating to 1983, when the restaurant opened in Keizer, are displayed in a glass case in the entryway. Team photo plaques decorate the walls and wood beams in the dining room, a mosaic of sponsorships and community connections. Empty spaces are noticeable on one beam, a sign that management is giving away plaques to family members of those in the photographs, including players who have since become parents, and coaches who have since passed. “They mean more to them,” said owner Christy Shores, daughter of JC’s founder Jim Campbell. The family-owned pizza parlor, known for its handmade dough and brick oven-style pizzas, has been a local hub for generations, a gathering place for youth sports teams and high school graduates and families celebrating birthdays, anniversaries and other milestones. Longtime customers were shocked and saddened to learn Shores was selling the building and closing the business. “No! It’s been a place of many celebrations,” one person posted on Facebook. The decision to sell was difficult for Shores but understandable. Her father died a little more than a year ago. She is the estate executor, spending more time these days with accountants and lawyers than with employees and customers. Her father, it turns out, was more of a real estate magnate than a pizza mogul. He amassed a property empire during his lifetime, including a bar, a 32-unit apartment complex, and 17 rental houses. All are aging and in need of more than just TLC. The pizza parlor at 4200 River Road N operates in a nearly 80-year-old building that Campbell purchased in the mid-1990s and hasn’t been regularly maintained or updated since. Shores chose a July 31 closing date because she knew she couldn’t make it through the summer with half of the 10 air conditioners on the roof of the 8,840-square-foot building out of commission. “I’m not closing because I have to close,” Shores said. “I’m closing because it’s the right time to close.” Jim Campbell ventured into the pizza business in 1982. He and a partner owned and operated Angelo’s on Commercial Street SE in the Candalaria Terrace Shopping Center. Angelo’s expanded into Keizer that fall and into Dallas the following spring, according to the Statesman Journal archives. The Keizer location opened in the former Orcutt’s Market building, built in 1947. Campbell became the sole owner of the Keizer location in 1983, renaming it JC’s Pizzaria. Dave Walery, of Walery’s Premium Pizza fame, had a hand in building the JC’s brand. Campbell convinced Walery, then working in Portland, to come and teach him everything he knew about making pizza. Years later, in a 2005 story about the business, Campbell told the Statesman Journal that he owed much of his success to Walery. “I had no pizza knowledge, and he gave me the recipes,” Campbell said. “Dave helped me out, and the rest is history.” No story about JC’s is complete without mention of the Keizer “pizza wars” in the mid-1980s between three outlets less than a mile apart on River Road N. Campbell launched the first salvo in 1984, dropping the price of a 16-inch pepperoni or Canadian bacon pizza to $3.99. He said he planned to rely on volume, and it worked. Competitors Abby’s Legendary Pizza and Dr. Munchie’s Incredible Pizza, started by Walery, counterattacked with their own similarly low-priced pizzas. The Statesman Journal published a 1986 story about the friendly competition, with photographs showing each owner taking a bite of a slice. The ultimate winners were pizza lovers in Keizer, Salem, and beyond. Shores worked for her father from the beginning when she was just 8 years old. She did everything from folding boxes and clearing tables to washing dishes and mopping floors. “This was home,” she said. “I felt like the employees helped raise me.” By age 14, she was in the kitchen making pizzas almost every day after school, on weekends, and during the summers. Trying to calculate just how many thousands of pizzas she has made in her lifetime is a dizzying prospect. By 16, she had the keys and was managing and closing the place. Those were the days when JC’s closed at 1 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays. It was the place to be after a McNary High School football game. “At 11 o’clock on a Friday night, there would be 400 people in here,” Shores said. Her brother worked there, too. But she was the one who took over operations in 2010, when her father stepped aside. "This has been my life," Shores said. JC’s has generally been open 363 days of the year, closing only on Thanksgiving and Christmas days. The longest stretch it was closed was for about three months in 2007 after a grease fire in the kitchen. The fire caused about $50,000 in damage, and the ovens had to be replaced. The secret to success for JC’s Pizzaria has been what Shores calls “old-school pizza.” “We still make our own dough, grind our own cheese, make our own sauce,” she said. “Everything is fresh.” The pizza lineup includes sports-themed names, such as the Quarterback (Canadian bacon, beef and tomatoes), the Umpire (mushrooms, green peppers, onions, beef and tomatoes), and the Bat Boy (cheese). For large groups, there’s the crowd-pleasing Giant Pizza, a carryover from the early days of Angelo’s. The price started at $100 and has increased to $450 today. The special-order pizza is 5 feet in diameter, weighs more than 70 pounds, and serves 40-60 people, making it popular for weddings, sports teams and Super Bowl parties. It also is the only pizza JC’s has ever delivered. When served in-house, it requires three people to carry it to a table. Campbell told the Statesman Journal in 2005 that he sold about 300 a year. A Giant Pizza must be ordered four days in advance, primarily because of the labor involved in making the dough and the required oven space. Shores said before the pandemic when dining in was more the norm, JC's served a minimum of five a week. The most she has served in a day is five, and she did that twice. “It’s not as popular as it used to be,” Shores said. Takeout orders have been a significant part of JC’s business over the years, ramping up during the pandemic. “We never closed and served to-go pizzas every day,” Shores said. “If I had my way, I’d have never reopened the lobby. I would have just done to-gos.” Since word spread about the impending closure, there has been an uptick in business. “But I’m never going to get back what it used to be,” Shores said. The countdown to closure has been a sentimental time for regular customers like Julio and Jazmin Navarro. They make the half-hour drive from Monmouth with their two young sons at least once a month. Shores happened to be working behind the counter during their most recent visit on a Friday afternoon and sliced their pizza just out of the oven. “Pepperoni and mushroom, and a side of fried mushrooms,” she said. “I can tell you their order, but I can’t tell you their names.” The Navarro family sat at a southwest corner table by the window, enjoying their usual order. They said they hope to squeeze in another visit or two before JC’s closes. “I did snap pictures when we got our food in case,” Julio Navarro said as 9-year-old Julian worked on his second slice. Some of the employees are just as nostalgic, whether they have worked at JC’s for a year or more than a decade. JC’s has employed hundreds, if not thousands, over the years, including many high school students working their first job. Some former employees have offered to return and help close. Shores remembers when she called Debbie Dederick, offering to help her friend out with a temporary job. What was supposed to be a 6-week gig filling in for an employee on maternity leave turned into 16 years. Dederick helps manage the place and is handling some of the logistics of closing, including finding homes for all those Little League photo plaques. (If you are connected with someone in one of the photos and would like the plaque as a keepsake, call JC's at 503-390-0805 and ask for a manager.) Dederick recently called the family that always sits at the table where the names Donna and Issah are etched in the surface, along with their funeral dates. She offered them the table and they plan to pick it up by closing day, but not before they gather around it one more time. The front windows are painted with the message “Thank you for 42 years!!" Shores said the JC's will close on July 31, whether the property sells by then. The building, listed by SVN Commercial Advisors , sits on nearly an acre and is advertised as “a rare opportunity to acquire one of Keizer’s most high-profile commercial sites.” The listing price is $2.5 million. The sale is for the property only, not the business. Shores is keeping the business name JC's Pizzaria and dreams of one day opening an express location, offering to-go orders only. She even has an eye on the perfect location. It cannot happen for at least a few years, until after her father’s estate has been settled, but the prospect makes her smile. Capi Lynn is a senior reporter for the Statesman Journal. Send comments, questions and tips to her at clynn@statesmanjournal.com , and follow her work on X @CapiLynn and Facebook @CapiLynnSJ.
